en.g: Use colour idioms like once in a blue moon, green with envy and out of the blue.
p: Once in a blue moon = very rarely. Out of the blue = suddenly, unexpectedly: She called me out of the blue.
Green with envy = very jealous (in a light way). Red tape = annoying official rules and paperwork.
In the red = owing money; in the black = making a profit. Caught red-handed = caught doing something wrong.
en.q: What is something you do only once in a blue moon? And what made you green with envy recently?
en.c: Tell a short story with three colour idioms from today, written or spoken.

de.q: Was machst du nur once in a blue moon? Und was hat dich zuletzt green with envy gemacht?
de.c: Erzähle eine kurze Geschichte mit drei Farb-Idiomen von heute, schriftlich oder mündlich.

es.q: ¿Qué haces solo once in a blue moon? ¿Y qué te puso green with envy hace poco?
es.c: Cuenta una historia corta con tres modismos de colores de hoy, por escrito o en voz alta.

en.g: Use body idioms like keep an eye on, cost an arm and a leg and get cold feet.
p: Keep an eye on = watch carefully. Cost an arm and a leg = be very expensive.
Pull someone's leg = joke with them. Get cold feet = become nervous and want to cancel a plan.
Break a leg = good luck (before a show). Learn by heart = memorise. Be all ears = listen eagerly.
en.q: Have you ever got cold feet before something important? What happened in the end?
en.c: Use four body idioms in a short message to a friend about a weekend plan.

en.g: Use idioms like time flies, in the nick of time and save for a rainy day.
p: Time flies (when you're having fun) = time passes quickly. In the nick of time = just before it's too late.
Save for a rainy day = keep money for future needs. Money doesn't grow on trees = money is limited.
Also: kill time (pass time while waiting), a bargain (good price), break the bank (cost too much).
en.q: When did you arrive somewhere in the nick of time? And how do you like to kill time while waiting?
en.c: Write three sentences about your week using time flies, in the nick of time and break the bank.

en.g: Use phrasal verbs with get: get over, get by, get away with, get across, get round to.
p: Get over = recover from: I got over my cold. Get by = manage with little: I get by with basic French.
Get away with = do something wrong without punishment. Get across = make an idea understood.
Get round to = finally find time for: I never get round to tidying my desk. Also: get on (with) = have a good relationship.
en.q: What is something you keep meaning to do but never get round to? And how do you get by in a new country?

en.t: Phrasal verbs with take and put
en.g: Use take up, take after, take on, put up with and put forward naturally.
p: Take up = start a hobby: I took up yoga. Take after = look or act like a parent: She takes after her dad.
Take on = accept work or responsibility: He took on a new project. Also take off = leave the ground or become popular.
Put up with = tolerate: I can't put up with noise. Put forward = suggest an idea: She put forward a plan.
en.q: What hobby would you like to take up, and who in your family do you take after?
en.c: Tell your Buddy about one thing you put up with and one idea you would put forward at work or school.

en.g: Use three-part phrasal verbs: look forward to, come up with, run out of, catch up on, get on with.
p: Three parts stay together, and the object goes at the end: I came up with an idea. We ran out of milk.
Look forward to + -ing: I look forward to meeting you. The to is a preposition, not part of the infinitive.
Catch up on = do something you missed: catch up on sleep. Get on with = continue: Let's get on with the meeting.
en.q: What are you looking forward to this month? And what do you need to catch up on?
en.c: Write a short note to a colleague using all five three-part phrasal verbs.

Look forward to + -ing: I look forward to meeting you. Das to ist eine Präposition, kein Infinitiv-to.
Catch up on = etwas nachholen: catch up on sleep. Get on with = weitermachen: Let's get on with the meeting.

Look forward to + -ing: I look forward to meeting you. El to es preposición, no parte del infinitivo.
Catch up on = ponerse al día con: catch up on sleep. Get on with = continuar: Let's get on with the meeting.

fr.g: Utilise des phrasal verbs en trois parties : look forward to, come up with, run out of, catch up on, get on with.
p: Les trois parties restent ensemble, le complément à la fin : I came up with an idea. We ran out of milk.
Look forward to + -ing : I look forward to meeting you. Le to est une préposition, pas celui de l'infinitif.
Catch up on = rattraper : catch up on sleep. Get on with = poursuivre : Let's get on with the meeting.
fr.q: Qu'est-ce que tu attends avec impatience ce mois-ci ? Et que dois-tu rattraper ?
fr.c: Écris un petit mot à un collègue avec les cinq phrasal verbs en trois parties.

it.g: Usa phrasal verbs in tre parti: look forward to, come up with, run out of, catch up on, get on with.
p: Le tre parti restano unite e l'oggetto va in fondo: I came up with an idea. We ran out of milk.
Look forward to + -ing: I look forward to meeting you. Il to è una preposizione, non quello dell'infinito.
Catch up on = recuperare: catch up on sleep. Get on with = andare avanti: Let's get on with the meeting.
it.q: Cosa non vedi l'ora di fare questo mese? E cosa devi recuperare?
it.c: Scrivi un breve messaggio a un collega usando tutti e cinque i phrasal verbs in tre parti.

pt.g: Usa phrasal verbs de três partes: look forward to, come up with, run out of, catch up on, get on with.
p: As três partes ficam juntas e o complemento vai no fim: I came up with an idea. We ran out of milk.
Look forward to + -ing: I look forward to meeting you. O to é preposição, não parte do infinitivo.
Catch up on = pôr em dia: catch up on sleep. Get on with = continuar: Let's get on with the meeting.
pt.q: O que estás ansioso por fazer este mês? E o que precisas de pôr em dia?
pt.c: Escreve uma nota curta a um colega com os cinco phrasal verbs de três partes.

pt_BR.g: Use phrasal verbs de três partes: look forward to, come up with, run out of, catch up on, get on with.
p: As três partes ficam juntas e o objeto vai no fim: I came up with an idea. We ran out of milk.
Look forward to + -ing: I look forward to meeting you. O to é preposição, não parte do infinitivo.
Catch up on = colocar em dia: catch up on sleep. Get on with = continuar: Let's get on with the meeting.

pt_BR.c: Escreva um bilhete curto a um colega usando os cinco phrasal verbs de três partes.

vocab.ex: I'm looking forward to seeing you on Friday.

It's hard to keep up with all the news.

target.gram: Three-part phrasal verbs are inseparable: object after the last particle. Look forward to is followed by -ing or a noun.

en.g: Use natural collocations: pay attention, take advantage, have a go, pay a compliment, take part.
p: Pay: pay attention, pay a compliment, pay a visit. Not make attention or give a compliment in this sense.
Take: take part, take advantage of, take a break, take a risk. Have: have a go, have a word, have fun.
Collocations are words that naturally go together. Learn them as chunks, not single words.
en.q: When did someone last pay you a nice compliment? And what would you like to have a go at?
en.c: Make one sentence each with pay attention, take part, take advantage of and have a go.

en.g: Use business collocations like meet a deadline, launch a product and reach an agreement.

en.g: Choose the right synonym for size: big, large, huge, enormous, vast.
p: Big is everyday and emotional: a big day, a big mistake. Large is neutral and formal: a large amount, large sizes.
Huge and enormous mean very big and sound stronger: a huge success, an enormous dog.
Vast is for wide areas or amounts: a vast desert, a vast majority. Don't say very huge; say absolutely huge.
en.q: What is the most enormous thing you have ever seen, and what was a big day in your life?

en.g: Stop mixing up affect/effect, borrow/lend, rise/raise and lose/loose.
p: Affect is a verb: Noise affects my sleep. Effect is usually a noun: Noise has an effect on my sleep.
Borrow = take for a while: Can I borrow your pen? Lend = give for a while: Can you lend me your pen?
Rise has no object: Prices rise. Raise needs one: Raise your hand. Lose = not find; loose = not tight.
en.q: Which of these pairs do you find most confusing, and how could you remember the difference?
en.c: Write four sentences, each using one pair correctly: affect/effect, borrow/lend, rise/raise, lose/loose.

de.g: Du verwechselst nicht mehr affect/effect, borrow/lend, rise/raise und lose/loose.
p: Affect ist ein Verb: Noise affects my sleep. Effect ist meist ein Nomen: Noise has an effect on my sleep.
Borrow = sich leihen: Can I borrow your pen? Lend = verleihen: Can you lend me your pen?
Rise ohne Objekt: Prices rise. Raise mit Objekt: Raise your hand. Lose = verlieren; loose = locker.
de.q: Welches Paar verwirrt dich am meisten, und wie könntest du dir den Unterschied merken?
de.c: Schreib vier Sätze, je einer pro Paar: affect/effect, borrow/lend, rise/raise, lose/loose.

es.q: ¿Qué pareja te confunde más y cómo podrías recordar la diferencia?
